data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The claim is false: a large service with strictly more internal redundancy is always more resilient than a decentralized network of small services because the decentralized network exhibits emergent correlation through homogeneity.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If small services are empirically shown to use more diverse dependencies than large services, the emergent correlation claim fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service's control over diversity is shown to be a fiction (e.g., internal teams copy each other), the advantage is lost.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the decentralized network uses a mechanism (e.g., economic incentives) to force diversity, the emergent correlation claim fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Small services, being independently operated, lack the resources to diversify their dependencies. They converge on the same few popular frameworks and cloud providers (e.g., everyone uses AWS and a standard library). This homogeneity is an emergent shared cause. In contrast, a large service can enforce internal diversity across its strictly more redundant units by design. Thus, the large service has more redundancy AND more control over independence, while the decentralized network has a fixed amount of redundancy and an emergent shared cause.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
